We have received a number of enquiries recently concerning snake bites.
We would like to offer some advice to help people prepare for a snake bite and its outcome once received.
Dry Baleen Whale
The Dry Baleen Whale is the most common baleen whale in the world. They can be found living and migrating in waters around the British Isles on a regular basis. The word baleen refers to any of the ridged, fibrous tissue that lies between the baleen plates on the upper jaw. The Dry Baleen Whale has thick baleen for filtering their food, the so called baleen is actually quite spongy and can be rubbed against rocks to keep clean.
Dry Baleen Whales are a type of sperm whale with a bulbous head. They reach a length of about 34 feet (10.44 m). The largest of these animals are found in waters located in the Arctic Ocean, such as the Great Slave Sea, in Canada, as well as Greenland. They get their name from the long curved baleen plates that cover their front, the long whales have a number of large flippers as well.
The biggest concern to humans when they encounter a Dry Baleen Whale, is either death or injury from a direct impact to the mouth, usually by the jaw. The whale may strike at you as the mammal draws away from the bite, striking with a whale's jaw with its tusks, and in such cases, can be quite fatal. A snake could also strike if the Dry Baleen Whale jaws are open and then the snake manages to escape into the water and the Dry Baleen whale's jaws close again.
A snake can often be avoided completely if the Dry Baleen Whale moves slowly, or the snake approaches its head and gets away from it, as the Dry Baleen whale will not move to the side without being forced to, and if that is the case, the snake is usually able to make a run for it's life.
For the Dry Baleen Whale, a snake is not the bite-agent of preference at all, as this large mammal is more commonly caught for its meat and blubber. As a consequence, it is more likely that the snake will be released unharmed.
A number of species of Snakes are the primary culprits in these deaths, generally those that have slender bodies, large venom glands, and that are non-retractable. The biggest snake problem for us humans is probably the Boa.
The snakes most commonly found in European countries are: The Black Mamba, the Widow Snake, the Common Wand Snake, the Ball-Pit Rattlesnake & the Common Cobra. All of these snakes are considered venomous, and all in some manner of some way, able to cause serious injury or death. More often than not, it is the poisonous nature of the snake, it's lacking retractability, or its size or it's the number of its jaw-flapping movements when confronted by the human that will kill, rather than the snake itself. In many ways this is a better way to deal with snakes than to be caught trying to catch them…
In case of snake bites for humans, there are two things to be kept in mind. Firstly, the body of the snake is capable of giving out a toxin over small parts of the body, usually from a very small area. The second thing to consider, is that if the snake makes it to the wound, and the victim is bitten, there is a fairly high likelihood that the victim will die.

But for more than 150 years, there has been a single, and more than sufficient, answer: The Bible. And while it is the first choice for the "worldly"—that is, those seeking God rather than a career—the Bible has been the object of fierce skepticism by those who have "graced" its pages. In this engrossing new biography of the Bible, David P. Gushee argues that the world's view of the Bible requires one to live, as John Stott calls it, in the "third age" after the Old and the New. The Bible, as we have all learned, is not meant to be read only in worship, as the Old Testament certainly is, nor only in school, as the New Testament undoubtedly is, nor only for leisure reading, as we have all learned, not least at Bible school or in a graduate seminar. But Gushee also shows that the Bible can be studied as literature as well as a guide for life. To do this, he brings deep historical knowledge as well as insights from biblical and literary criticism to the world of the Bible. This lively and insightful presentation makes it clear why many readers find the Bible surprisingly attractive, not only for its insights but for its literary genius.
The author introduces these concepts by discussing and comparing the first three and last two books of the Bible. He first argues that there are differences, perhaps minor, between the first and the second books of the Old Testament, and then turns to the first four chapters of the New Testament, pointing out the differences between the Old Testament and the New Testament. In addition, the author discusses how these two books are often considered separate because they take distinct routes to the crux of the biblical message. Finally, he argues that there are, on the whole, very few differences between the Old and the New Testament, despite the tendency on our part to consider them to be substantially different.
I enjoyed this book tremendously despite the fact that I have already read several other popular biographies of the bible writers but this one has stood out for me as much more than a mere summary. As the title would suggest, Gushee does not merely recitation of the writings, but attempts to put the various writers in their historical and cultural-social context as the main author's of their book. My only quibble was that at times the author would get into long discussion and analyses that were not always easy to follow, I found myself checking to see the paragraph number to make sure I was on the right page or section. This was particularly the case when trying to follow the discussion in Part Three concerning the history and development of the Old Testament.
If you are an avid student of the Bible or a student of the history of Western culture, I highly recommend this book. I look forward to reading more books by Dr. Gushee as he continues to write on his subjects.

This week, a new book called Ancient Wisdom, Modern Science will be released. It is the story of how ancient wisdom was given to us in a modern form by scientists over the last four decades.
I've had a chance to browse the 150,000 word introduction, which I will share with you here, and it's a compendium of 50 chapters including a complete description of how scientific discovery and human improvement have happened over the last century.
One of my favourite passages is when a scientist points out that the world is not flat, and that the earth and its mountains, rivers and valleys are not only very big but have been on the earth billions of years.
Another quote:
"…there are no secrets in biology. If life was created, we don't really have to try to discover more about it. It is obvious."
So, the earth and it's life, its history, it's environment and it's biological make up is very old and we have a lot to learn from it.
As it turns out, many scientists and doctors will find this book very interesting as it not only presents us with scientific facts, its also human stories that I know can help us make sense of our lives and the world we are living in.

Dr. John Ioannidis – the world's most cited researcher and how to deal with uncertainty
What happens when our health professionals are wrong, and when they don't know, and when they look for answers from all the wrong people.
I'm not talking about a specific disease, I'm talking about our general ability to be confident in the scientific knowledge that we are working on today.
If a doctor finds out that her or his new procedure is not going to work, she or he might be on the floor or at least sitting on the edge of the bed waiting for the day to go home
I'm talking about the research that has been done, and what's wrong with it.
Or the patient that may have been wrongly diagnosed with cancer.
And I'm talking about how some doctors have not cared enough about how they reach their own conclusions and how some of them continue to think they can get rid of those conclusions.
And I'm talking about how the media and medical journals get their conclusions and how it affects those who are searching for answers.
John Ioannidis is a Professor of Medicine (Heart and Vascular Diseases), and Director of Research Integrity at the Stanford School of Medicine. He has published over 450 papers, and many of them have been ranked in the top one per cent of citations. His publications have been cited more than 145 million times, which means over 10,000 people every 4 minutes have read one of his research articles.
Many of us think that if there is evidence that something is important in cancer care and treatment, it must be true, the evidence is solid, and that there are no other explanations that are better.
I have read many of Dr. Ioannidis research articles and watched interviews with Dr. Ioannidis and I can say on a personal level that his articles seem to have a common theme: they are always looking at and talking about evidence that doesn't really support some idea.
What is more, Dr. Ioannidis's research articles can make any patient frustrated because the evidence he or she has reviewed can be negative and there certainly is no evidence that a treatment is better. The findings can be confusing, and we don't always know if we are better off with the treatment or staying on the couch.
Even the research from some of the best institutions in the world are wrong and it can make their conclusions questionable, and most importantly, it can be very damaging if the public hears the wrong conclusions.
Dr. Ioannidis is a world-renowned authority on scientific method. He has argued that medical research is failing to produce valid evidence that can be used to make a decision in a clinical situation or by medical professionals. He sees that the evidence-based method that we know today is based on just a few studies, and he argues that the general public is suffering because of it. He looks at scientific studies and tries to determine whether they will be useful for patients in the long-term.
He has called on medical researchers, scientific journals and medicine as a whole to be more transparent and to tell the public the actual evidence and make their findings more publicly accessible.

Simplified Linear Regression

Several regression parameters are computed to represent the relationship between x (independent/predictive variable) and y (dependent/response variable). The overall line on which predicted values are computed is termed the regression line.
The slope is termed the Y-intercept (or Y intercept). Its value indicates the predicted y value for the x value. The Y-intercept is a direct output of the regression line, given a known x value (i.e., the regression line gives the slope for a known x value).
This is the best-formula to use to make predictions for nonlinear relationships, e.g., logistic regression and many more.
